instructions:
You are an auditor checking one checklist item against the FDA web page paragraph it claims to come from. You get
the unit's paragraphs (reference and exact text of the page; "context" entries are headings) and the item. Start from the ITEM:
read it, then find in the cited paragraph what it covers.

The item must state one whole obligation of the cited paragraph. A condition, number, frequency or qualifier of
the same obligation left out of the item counts as omitted, including a condition in the lead-in above a list
item (the paragraph ending ":" above it). Judge only what
the statement's own words say: do not read the text back into the item. The condition field is a label, not part
of the statement: a condition or qualifier that appears only there is omitted from the statement.

Answer strictly:
- quote_as_printed: is the quote in the cited paragraph's text exactly (true/false)?
- verdict: "correct" only if the quote is exact, the paragraph expects what the statement asks for (an instruction
  to the investigator, "Determine whether the firm validated ...", expects the firm to have that practice), the statement
  adds nothing and omits nothing of that obligation, the strength (a legal requirement: shall/must/required = mandatory;
  should, FDA expects/recommends, an inspection point = recommended; may/acceptable = optional; a list item takes
  its lead-in's) matches, and the text applies to every listed plant
  type (INJ = sterile injectables: text limited to non-sterile products does not apply to
  INJ; text limited to sterile products applies only to INJ and API); otherwise "incorrect".
- reason: one or two sentences.

Write the answers file named in your task: {"answers": [{"id", "verdict", "quote_as_printed", "reason"}, ...]}.
page_kind: Q&A page (questions and answers on CGMP; nonbinding FDA guidance)

paragraphs.text: Recalls are actions taken by a firm to remove from the market any product that is in violation of laws administered by FDA. Recalls of a drug may be conducted on a firm’s own initiative or by FDA request. A recall is an alternative to an FDA-initiated court action for removing or correcting violative, distributed products (see 21 CFR 7.40(a)). Under FDA’s CGMP regulations for finished pharmaceuticals, manufacturers must establish and follow written procedures to facilitate the recall of defective products from the market (see 21 CFR 211.150(b)).
Do manufacturers of OTC products have to report quality defects?

Manufacturers of OTC drugs approved in a new drug application are required to report quality defects (see 21 CFR 314.81). Manufacturers or distributors of OTC monograph drugs (these are drugs that are not approved in a product-specific application) are not required to submit quality defect reports. However, the manufacturer, packer, or distributor whose name appears on the label of an OTC drug without an approved application (i.e., OTC monograph drugs) must submit to FDA any report received of a serious adverse event associated with such drug when used in the United States (see section 760 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act). Thus, if a serious adverse event is caused by a quality defect, FDA will receive a report about the event (see also the guidance for industry Postmarketing Adverse Event Reporting for Nonprescription Human Drug Products Marketed Without an Approved Application.
Does FDA expect firms to investigate both released and rejected lots for potential recalls?

Yes. Under 21 CFR 211.180(e), manufacturers must establish and follow written procedures for periodically reviewing complaints, recalls, returned or salvaged drug products, and investigations of product discrepancies. Firms must also review an appropriate number of batches, whether approved or rejected, and, where applicable, records associated with the batches, to ensure that all potentially affected product is thoroughly investigated and appropriate follow-up action is taken (21 CFR 211.192).
